2611.25079.abstract: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) continues to identify thousands of transit candidates that require statistical validation to rule out astrophysical false positives before atmospheric characterization can be pursued. We statistically validate and characterize seven TESS exoplanet candidates orbiting five host stars. As a consistency check of our automated vetting and Bayesian inference pipeline, we include TOI-2392.03, a sub-Neptune companion previously validated in the literature. Our framework combines automated signal retrieval, pixel-level centroid and Gaia DR3 contamination analysis, and false positive probability (FPP) computation with the TRICERATOPS vetting engine. Physical and orbital parameters are derived via nested sampling (juliet/Dynesty), complemented by an empirical mass-radius relation, since no dynamical mass measurements are available. Applying the same procedure to all candidates, we statistically validate six new exoplanets ($\mathrm{FPP} < 0.015$ and $\mathrm{NFPP} < 0.001$), one of which (TOI-7721.01) lies close to the FPP threshold. We report the period ratios of the three-planet system TOI-2392, and identify TOI-7721.01 and TOI-1277.02 as the candidates with the highest Transmission Spectroscopy Metrics (TSM) in our sample, making them targets of interest for atmospheric follow-up with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the upcoming Ariel mission.

2611.25120.abstract: The eccentricity of an exoplanet's orbit is a key observational quantity that can be used to infer its dynamical past and predict its future orbital evolution. Planets are expected to emerge from their protoplanetary cradles with roughly circular eccentricities, and non-circular eccentricites to arise from subsequent dynamical processing in the absence of the gas disk. We present an updated orbit for 51 Eridani b based on 5 years of 0.2 mas precision optical interferometry from VLTI/GRAVITY(+). This planet is young (${\sim}20\,\mathrm{Myr}$ old), temperate ($T_{\rm eff}\sim650\,\mathrm{K}$), and on a wide orbit ($a{=}9.36\,\mathrm{au}$) with an uncertain mass ($M_{\rm b}\leq12\,M_{\rm J}$). We measured the planet's motion to an exceptionally high precision, confirming that its orbit is very eccentric ($e_b=0.574\pm0.003$). We observe residuals to the absolute astrometry of the host star based on a single planet orbit that could be attributable to reflex motion from a third body in the system. We construct a two companion orbit model that could explain the apparent reflex motion of 51 Eri A: this model predicts that the putative second companion has $M_c\in[1.0, 2900]_{95\%}\,M_{\rm Jup}$ and $a_c\in[0.3, 3.1]_{95\%}\,\mathrm{au}$. In this framework, a dynamical interaction between b and ``c" could have kicked the exterior, lower mass b out onto its present, eccentric orbit. If this signal is astrophysical, and not due to a systematic error, this candidate should be confirmable with Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry in the near future.

Figure 4: Schematic illustration of the two post-circularization scenarios for WASP-12 b. In both scenarios, the planet undergoes high-eccentricity migration and reaches a highly eccentric orbit with pericenter distance $r_{\rm peri}$. Tidal circularization approximately conserves orbital angular momentum, producing a circular orbit with semimajor axis $a_{\rm final}\simeq 2r_{\rm peri}$. Left—Scenario 1: Inflation by circularization. The planet has reached approximately its current radius ($R_{p}\simeq 1.89~R_{\rm Jup}$) by circularization. Its low mean density places the Roche limit farther from the star, yielding a post-circularization period of approximately 2.97 d. Right—Scenario 2: Inflation by irradiation after circularization. The planet remains relatively compact ($R_{p}\simeq 1.10~R_{\rm Jup}$) during circularization. Its higher density gives a smaller Roche limit and a post-circularization period of approximately 1.32 d. The planet subsequently inflates as tidal evolution brings it to the present-day orbital period of 1.09 d and radius of $R_{p}\simeq 1.89~R_{\rm Jup}$. The two scenarios therefore provide substantially different amounts of orbital angular momentum for transfer during subsequent inspiral.

Figure 5: Schematic illustration of angular-momentum transfer between WASP-12 b and its host star using a hydraulic analogy. The upper and lower panels show an illustrative initially retrograde configuration and the present-day prograde configuration, respectively. Reservoir widths represent effective moments of inertia, and fluid levels represent angular frequencies. Here, $\Omega>0$ and $\Omega<0$ denote prograde and retrograde rotation relative to the planetary orbit, respectively. The three reservoirs represent the planetary orbit ($L_{\rm orb}$), the stellar convective envelope ($J_{\rm env}$), and the stellar interior beneath the convective envelope ($J_{\rm int}$). The stellar interior and planetary orbit are much larger angular-momentum reservoirs than the convective envelope. Orbital angular momentum may be deposited into the convective envelope at a rate $\dot{J}_{\rm pl\rightarrow env}$ and subsequently redistributed into the stellar interior at a rate $\dot{J}_{\rm env\rightarrow int}$. Direct deposition into the stellar interior is also possible. In the retrograde-to-prograde scenario discussed in Section IV.3, tidal transfer first cancels the initially retrograde stellar spin and then drives the star into the present prograde configuration while the planetary orbit loses angular momentum.

2611.25203.abstract: WASP-12 b is the only exoplanet with confirmed orbital decay. Angular momentum transferred from its decaying orbit should have realigned the star's thin convective layer, yet an earlier Rossiter--McLaughlin (RM) measurement suggested a $\sim$60$^\circ$ spin--orbit misalignment. We present two new Keck Planet Finder RM measurements. We measure a sky-projected obliquity of $\lambda=-1.3\pm8.7^\circ$; and the star's projected rotation velocity is $v\sin i_\star=1.3\pm0.1~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, an order of magnitude lower than expected for a star of its mass and age. With WASP-12's low chromospheric activity, $\log R^\prime_{\rm HK}=-5.5$, our analysis favors an aligned system in which $v\sin i_\star$ reflects slow surface rotation with $P_{\rm rot}\sim60$ days, rather than a projection effect. Our evolution models favor a late-main-sequence star rather than a subgiant, with a central convective core found in 99\% of posterior samples. This internal structure suppresses the central-focusing and nonlinear wave-breaking mechanisms for inward-propagating gravity waves. We propose that WASP-12 b was initially placed on a retrograde orbit after high-eccentricity migration, when its host rotated at $v\sin i_\star\approx14$~km~s$^{-1}$ (or $P_{\rm rot}\sim$6 days). Tidal decay transferred orbital angular momentum to the convective envelope, aligning the surface. The retrograde interior acts as an angular-momentum reservoir, while interior--envelope coupling slows the surface rotation. A semi-empirical relation gives an envelope--interior angular-momentum exchange timescale of $\sim4$~Myr, similar to the observed orbital-decay timescale of $\sim3.25$~Myr. The angular-momentum budget also permits this initially retrograde evolution. In contrast, an initially prograde planet would have spun up the surface rotation to a rate substantially higher than observed.

2611.25230.abstract: Among the current population of exoplanets there are very few sub-Neptunes that have their atmospheric composition identified. This is primarily due to sub-Neptunes having high metallicity, clouds, and/or hazes obscuring absorption features. This often produces a spectrum that presents itself as a featureless spectrum especially in the near-IR. However, there are tentative trends that suggest sub-Neptunes with the lowest equilibrium temperatures ($\mathrm{T_{eq} < 400\:K}$) have detectable features, perhaps due to inefficient haze production or cloud sedimentation. TOI-6478 b is a low-density sub-Neptune exoplanet ($\rm <\mathrm{9.9\:M_{\oplus}}$ and $\rm \sim 4.5R_{\oplus}$) with an equilibrium temperature $\mathrm{T_{eq} = 220 \:K}$ assuming zero albedo. In this study, we present the highest S/N spectral feature ($\sim$6) of any sub-Neptune detected using HST/WFC3. We detect this spectral feature using a robust analysis that incorporates the Transit Light Source Effect (TLSE) to rule out false detections due to stellar activity. With the narrow bandpass of HST we were unable to distinguish whether the spectral feature at 1.4$\mu$m is from H$_2$O or CH$_4$ absorption. Meanwhile, self-consistent atmospheric models provide physical motivation for CH$_4$ to be the dominant absorber given that H$_2$O should condense or cold trap at higher pressures. Through our analysis we determine that HST/WFC3 alone cannot distinguish between major absorbers. However, a broader wavelength coverage by JWST will be able to measure the atmospheric composition in detail, due to the high S/N features for this target.

2611.25255.abstract: Venus and Earth, planets with similar masses and radii, provide astonishingly different environments, raising the question of why these two rocky worlds evolved so differently. Explaining this divergence is a central challenge in comparative planetology and astrobiology. Now, atmospheric studies of exoplanets can explore the possibilities of terrestrial planet evolution, especially in the era of JWST; however, we have not yet realized the critical insights rocky exoplanets in the Transition Zone (TZ) can provide. These TZ planets in the overlap between the Habitable Zone and Venus Zone can test how incident stellar irradiation affects surface water retention and habitability. Observations of exoplanets in the TZ can probe not only the emergence and decline of exoplanet habitability but also test hypotheses about Venus' past, complementing upcoming Venus flagship missions. Here, we analyze NASA's Exoplanet Archive, updated with Gaia DR3 data, and provide a target list of 23 rocky exoplanets in the Earth-to-Venus Transition Zone, along with 2 planets in the Venus Evolution Zone (EV). We examine their demographics and quantify their potential for follow-up observations. This list of rocky TZ and EV planets allows observers to optimize target selection and observing strategy for specific instruments. Characterizing exoplanets in the Transition Zone will be critical to investigating open questions about the emergence and decline of habitability on rocky worlds, the evolution from an exo-Earth to an exo-Venus, and Earth's future.

2611.25602.abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.

2611.25803.abstract: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics. This study specifically examines whether clouds explain the systematically low nightside brightness observed in Spitzer thermal phase curves of ultra-hot Jupiters. We found that clouds generally increase phase-curve amplitudes and reduce eastward offsets, and these effects are most pronounced at relatively low T_eq and gradually weaken as T_eq increases. We discussed two mechanisms responsible for reducing the phase-curve offsets by clouds: the dynamical and geometric effects. Without explicit dissipation of large-scale winds, strong equatorial jets develop, maintaining a hot equatorial region and clearing clouds near the nightside equator at T_eq >= 2200 K, with thick clouds instead forming mainly at mid-to-high latitudes. These patchy nightside clouds do not sustain low nightside fluxes as temperatures rise, suggesting that clouds alone cannot explain the observed nightside brightness for ultra-hot Jupiters. Strong dissipation, parameterized as magnetic drags, suppresses equatorial jets and promotes nightside cloud coverage. In both clear and cloudy models, drag weakens the dependence of Spitzer nightside brightness temperature on equilibrium temperature; clouds further lower the nightside brightness temperature with the same drag prescription. Clouds also dampen amplitudes of thermal spectra on the nightside and, under small-particle conditions, can even produce emission features. Due to limited dayside cloud cover, our models yield negligible Bond albedos. Finally, interpreting simulated thermal phase curves with energy balance models in near-IR and IR bands tends to overestimate the Bond albedos of ultra-hot Jupiters by an order of magnitude or more.

2611.26025.title: The Ionospheric Cut-off as a Potential Radio Technosignature

figures.caption: Figure 1: The phase-independent turnover. The fraction of surface-origin continuum emission that escapes to a distant observer is shown as a function of frequency for two targets of Table 2: the Sun–Earth case ($u_{c}^{\rm noon}=10$ MHz) and a planet in the habitable zone of AD Leo ($u_{c}^{\rm noon}=38$ MHz). The lines show the orbit-averaged escape fraction of the fiducial disc-integrated model developed in Section 5.2 (equation 17); the shaded bands show the range covered over the orbit, from the transit (nightside) spectrum on the left to the eclipse (dayside) spectrum on the right. The turnover moves within the band but is present at every phase. The change of slope near the half-escape level is a consequence of the sharp per-element step adopted in the model, and would be smoothed in a real ionosphere (see Fig. 3).

Figure 2: Viewing geometry of the phase-locked cut-off.
Panel (a): the orbit viewed from above the orbital plane, with the
observer towards the bottom. At secondary eclipse ($\phi=0$) the dayside
hemisphere faces the observer; at transit ($\phi=0.5$) the nightside faces
the observer; quadrature ($\phi=0.25$) presents half of each.
Panel (b): the visible disc as seen by the observer at the same
three phases, shaded by the local cut-off
$u_{c}^{\rm loc}/u_{c}^{\rm noon}=[\max(\cos\chi,\xi)]^{1/4}$
(equation 14). The greyscale represents the local ionospheric cut-off, not reflected-light brightness. The substellar point (S) sits at the disc centre at
eclipse but is projected onto the limb at quadrature, where the terminator
(dashed) crosses the disc centre; at transit, the disc sits uniformly at the
nightside floor $\xi^{1/4}\approx 0.47$ (the uniform shade reflects the
single-valued floor $\xi$, which subsumes dusk-to-dawn structure into one
number; Section 5.3 relaxes this assumption). The visible disc
thus spans the full range of local cut-offs at quadrature, but a single value
at transit – which is why the disc-integrated turnover is broadest at
quadrature and narrowest at transit (though not sharp: once the dependence of the escape threshold on the emission angle towards the observer is included, Section 5.2, elements near the limb escape only at higher frequencies at every phase).

Figure 3: Disc-integrated escape model including the observer-directed escape threshold (equation 17), for the Earth-calibrated nightside floor $\xi=0.05$, zero obliquity, an edge-on orbit, and uniform intrinsic leakage.
Panel (a): the half-escape frequency $u_{1/2}(\phi)$ as a function of orbital phase ($\phi=0$ at superior conjunction). Solid: the fiducial model (thin-shell obliquity factor with $h/R=0.047$ and Lambertian emission weighting $w=\mu$). Dashed: the plane-parallel secant law $S=1/\mu$, for which the eclipse and transit values are analytic, $2^{3/8}\approx 1.30$ and $\sqrt{2}\,\xi^{1/4}\approx 0.67$. Dot–dashed: isotropic emitters ($w=1$). Dotted: the vertical-incidence proxy $\langleu_{c}\rangle$ of equation (15), which spans $8/9$ to $\xi^{1/4}$. Including the observer-directed threshold raises the level of $u_{1/2}$ by $\approx 40$ per cent and produces a flat plateau at the nightside value for $|\phi-0.5|\lesssim 0.13$, but leaves the fractional modulation $A=(u_{1/2}^{\max}-u_{1/2}^{\min})/u_{1/2}^{\max}$ essentially unchanged: 48 per cent for the fiducial and plane-parallel models, against 47 per cent for the proxy; isotropic and horizon-peaked emission give 44 and 39 per cent.
Panel (b): the escape fraction $f_{\rm esc}(u,\phi)$ of the fiducial model at eclipse, quadrature and transit, with a sharp per-element step; the horizontal line marks $f_{\rm esc}=\tfrac{1}{2}$. At eclipse no leakage escapes below $u_{c}^{\rm noon}$, because every element must satisfy $u\gequ_{c}^{\rm loc}S(\mu)\gequ_{c}^{\rm noon}$; the extended high-frequency tails arise from elements near the limb. The sharp onset at $u_{c}^{\rm noon}$ and the steep rise near $1.9\,u_{c}^{\rm noon}$ in the eclipse curve arise from the sharp
per-element step and the infinitely thin shell: the observer-directed
threshold peaks at $\approx 1.90\,u_{c}^{\rm noon}$ near $\mu\approx 0.18$
and falls again towards the limb. In a real ionosphere these features would be rounded off by finite layer thickness, refraction, magnetoionic splitting (of order $u_{B}/2$), and collisional absorption (Section 2), with little effect on $u_{1/2}$.

Figure 4: Time-dependent generalisation of the cut-off model, from the non-dimensional form of equation (18) (Section 5.3), for a solar day $P_{\rm sol}=1$ d and prograde rotation. Three cases are shown: the equilibrium limit $\varepsilon\to 0$ (solid), which also describes synchronously rotating planets; a fast response, $\varepsilon=\tau_{\rm eff}/P_{\rm sol}=0.025$ ($\tau_{\rm eff}\approx 36$ min; dashed); and a slow response, $\varepsilon=0.1$ ($\tau_{\rm eff}\approx 2.4$ h; dot–dashed), closer to the behaviour of Earth’s F2 peak.
Panel (a): the steady-state local cut-off at the equator as a function of local time. A finite response time carries near-daytime densities past dusk, so that the nightside minimum is reached only just before dawn.
Panel (b): the corresponding half-escape frequency $u_{1/2}(\phi)$ as a function of orbital phase, computed with the fiducial obliquity factor and Lambertian emission weighting of Fig. 3. The equilibrium curve is symmetric about transit. A finite response displaces the curve in the direction of rotation: the maximum lags superior conjunction by $\Delta\phi\approx 0.02$ (fast) and $0.07$ (slow), and the centre of the nightside plateau lags transit by $\approx 0.05$ and $0.15$ respectively. The fractional modulation $A=(u_{1/2}^{\max}-u_{1/2}^{\min})/u_{1/2}^{\max}$ is 48 per cent for the equilibrium and fast-response cases and 42 per cent for the slow response. In all cases the period of the modulation remains the orbital period.

2611.26025.abstract: Radio emission generated on a planetary surface must cross the planet's ionosphere before escaping into space: below the local plasma frequency it is reflected back towards the surface. We investigate this process for broadband radio technosignatures (BRaTs) using a Chapman-layer description of photoionised atmospheres. The plasma frequency depends only weakly on stellar XUV irradiation, scaling as $Q_{\infty}^{1/4}$, implying turnover frequencies of 5-40 MHz for most terrestrial habitable-zone planets, potentially rising towards 100 MHz in extreme environments. The basic signature is simple: the continuum of a surface-origin BRaT should be strongly suppressed below a characteristic frequency that can be estimated from the XUV output of the host star, at every orbital phase and for any viewing geometry. Oblique propagation, magnetic fields, and collisional absorption broaden the cut-off into a smooth escape function, $f_{\mathrm{esc}}(u,\phi)$, where $\phi$ is the orbital phase. Because the day-night ionisation pattern is anchored to the substellar point rather than to the rotating surface, disc integration adds a second, more discriminating signature: the half-escape frequency $u_{1/2}$ varies predictably (by about 40-50 per cent over the orbit, depending on the angular emission pattern of the leakage) and remains locked to the orbital ephemeris. Finite atmospheric response times introduce modest phase lags but preserve the modulation. A low-frequency turnover alone is not unique to technology, but one that varies periodically with the orbital period would be difficult to reproduce through known astrophysical processes. Although observationally challenging, the ionospheric cut-off is a potential technosignature diagnostic and a novel probe of exoplanet ionospheres.

2611.26372.abstract: The survival of an inner planet next to a close-in giant is commonly used to argue against high-eccentricity migration (HEM), because the eccentric giant is expected to destabilize the inner system. Existing survival calculations have concentrated on Jupiter-mass migrants, although several Jupiter-sized close-in giants with nearby companions have sub-Jovian masses. We use dissipative three-body integrations to measure the collision-survival boundary at seven giant masses from $0.25$ to $1.0,M_{\rm Jup}$ and combine it with uncompressed equilibrium-tide circularization times. At fixed physical periapse, lower giant mass weakens the forcing of the inner orbit and shifts the survival boundary inward. It also shortens the circularization time for a common radius and tidal prescription. These dynamical and tidal limits enclose a viable HEM region in which a sub-Jovian giant can circularize within a system age while retaining an ultra-short-period companion. We screen known companion-hosting close-in giants and perform system-specific integrations of WASP-132; every current candidate lies outside the region. A future system inside it would show directly that HEM can produce a close-in giant while preserving an inner planet, converting companion survival into positive evidence for this formation channel.

2611.26548.title: Demographic inference in exoplanet chemistry is shaped by retrieval assumptions

2611.26548.abstract: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history. Atmospheric C/O can provide clues about where and how planets form, particularly through the accretion of gas and solids across disk snowlines. Since planetary migration can change orbital distances and hence equilibrium temperatures ($T_{eq}$), investigating C/O across different planetary populations may provide insights into their formation and evolution. As observational precision improves with the JWST, the limits of standard atmospheric retrieval methods that assume altitude-independent molecular abundances have become apparent. We present atmospheric retrievals for 20 transiting planets with published JWST transmission spectra, including complementary HST spectra for targets where such data are available, spanning gas giants, warm Neptunes, and temperate/warm sub-Neptunes, to test how population-level chemical inferences depend on retrieval assumptions. Free-chemistry retrievals show a visually non-monotonic C/O-$T_{eq}$ distribution, but this apparent pattern is not statistically robust and is sensitive to sample composition. When molecular abundances are constrained by a grid of disequilibrium models, the inferred C/O distribution becomes more restricted, showing that demographic chemical trends can depend strongly on the adopted retrieval parameterization. Several hot Jupiters converge to low C/O ($\leq$ 0.05), whereas colder, cloudy planets retain broad posteriors that reflect limited information content of their spectra. Our results suggest that population-level chemical trends inferred from free-chemistry retrievals should be interpreted with caution unless sample selection, residual structure, prior sensitivity, and chemical assumptions are explicitly tested.
